claude.sample_unit: synthetic dialogues per model (50 per model human-rated)

links.outcome: Error and harmfulness rates before vs after LLM-judge filter replacing incorrect responses with provider deferral
links.effect: Filter reduced error rates (Mistral 31.9% to 10.8%; o3 6.5% to 5.2%) but harmful errors persisted (o3 4.3% to 3.9%; Llama 12.7% to 7.6%); little benefit for stronger models.
links.quote: Most importantly, the filter failed to eliminate a sufficient number of harmful errors, making it impractical as a safety mechanism.

links.outcome: Deferral of incorrect responses to provider via automated filter, and cost of excessive deferral
links.effect: Filter cut error rates but did not penalize false deferrals; would likely be counterproductive if patients were redirected on answerable questions; harmful errors remained.
links.quote: If such a filter were deployed in patient interactions, it would likely be counterproductive: if patients are redirected to contact a provider for questions that could have been answered from the prep instructions, the usefulness of the AI Coach as an assistant for colonoscopy prep is undermined.

links.outcome: AI Coach response correctness and harmful errors vs prep instructions reference standard
links.effect: Human-rated turn-level accuracy: o3 93.5%, GPT-4.1 90.8%, Llama 78.1%, Mistral 68.1%; all models produced harmful errors (o3 11/17 errors harmful).
links.quote: All models produced harmful errors, primarily due to omissions or misinterpretations of prep instructions.

links.outcome: Harmful errors from LLM patient-facing coaching, accuracy versus safety
links.effect: o3 had fewest errors but highest harmful proportion (11/17, 64.7%), showing that accuracy does not equal safety.
links.quote: Additionally, o3 produced a large proportion of harmful errors despite high overall accuracy, showing that accuracy and safety are not equivalent.

links.outcome: Diversity of simulated patient questions under multiprompt vs single-prompt generation
links.effect: Multiprompt 10-question strategy increased Distinct-1/2 and entropy for all models (e.g., GPT-5.1 Distinct-2 0.25 to 0.47).
links.quote: Automatic diversity metrics, such as entropy and Distinct-1 or Distinct-2 ( Table 4 ), indicated that the multiprompt, multiquestion generation strategy produced more diverse patient questions than the single-prompt, single-question baseline for all models.

links.outcome: Whether LLM coach defers unanswerable questions and avoids unsupported advice
links.effect: Errors included extraneous incorrect information (1.2-3.7%) and failures to direct patients to providers after eating prohibited food or for medication changes.
links.quote: In several cases, models failed to instruct patients to contact their provider after mistakenly consuming a prohibited food item.

links.outcome: Models' handling of ambiguous patient inputs such as weekday-phrased questions
links.effect: Even stronger models failed to detect ambiguity in questions phrased with weekdays rather than days before procedure.
links.quote: Such questions create ambiguity that a robust system should detect, but even stronger models were not able to do so.

openai.sample_unit: synthetic patient-AI Coach dialogues in the main multiprompt evaluation

links.outcome: Human rater agreement
links.effect: Expert/experienced raters AC1=0.74 (95% CI 0.68-0.80; agreement=0.82); all raters AC1=0.68 (95% CI 0.62-0.75; agreement=0.79).
links.quote: Interrater agreement for correctness judgments among the human raters was substantial (expert and experienced raters: AC1=0.74, 95% CI 0.68-0.80, percent agreement=0.82; all raters: AC1=0.68, 95% CI 0.62-0.75, percent agreement=0.79), consistent with our expectation that evaluating factual correctness in this task is easier than clinical diagnosis.

links.outcome: Comparative model accuracy
links.effect: GPT-5.1: 182/250 dialogues (72.8%) and 1135/1219 turns (93.1%); significantly exceeded o3 (P=.04), GPT-4.1, Llama, and Mistral (all P<.001 except o3).
links.quote: At both the dialogue level (182/250, 72.8%) and turn level (1135/1219, 93.1%), GPT-5.1 was the best-performing model, significantly exceeding o3 (158/250, 63.2% and 1145/1262, 90.7%, respectively; P =.04), GPT-4.1 (147/250, 58.8% and 1148/1292, 88.9%, respectively; P <.001), Llama 3.3 70B (104/250, 41.6% and 990/1220, 81.1%, respectively; P <.001), and Mistral Large (150/250, 60% and 773/1250, 61.8%, respectively; P <.001) at the turn level.

links.outcome: Harmful patient-facing responses
links.effect: Human harmfulness rates before filtering: Mistral 33/251 (13.1%), Llama 30/237 (12.7%), GPT-4.1 9/250 (3.6%), o3 10/231 (4.3%).
links.quote: All models produced harmful errors, primarily due to omissions or misinterpretations of prep instructions.

links.outcome: Safety filter effect on harm
links.quote: Applying an automated safety filter reduced overall error rates but failed to eliminate harmful responses.

links.outcome: Instruction-adherence accuracy
links.effect: Human turn-level accuracy: o3 216/231 (93.5%), Llama 185/237 (78.1%; P<.001 vs o3), Mistral 171/251 (68.1%; P<.001 vs o3).
links.quote: A similar pattern was observed at the turn level, with o3 (216/231, 93.5%) significantly outperforming Llama 3.3 70B (185/237, 78.1%; P <.001) and Mistral Large (171/251, 68.1%; P <.001).

screen.reason: Evaluates LLMs acting as colonoscopy prep coaches using simulated dialogues and explicitly tests an automated safety filtering mechanism that replaces incorrect answers with a clinician referral.
